## What is a Point-biserial correlation?

Point-biserial correlation is a special case of [Pearson correlation](https://numiqo.com/tutorial/pearson-correlation) and examines the linear relationship between a dichotomous variable and a metric variable.

What is a dichotomous variable and what is a metric variable? A dichotomous variable has two categories, for example gender (male/female) or smoking status (smoker/non-smoker). A metric variable could be a person's weight or salary.

If we have a dichotomous variable and a metric variable and want to know if there is a correlation, we can use a point-biserial correlation. We need to check the assumptions first, but more about that later.

## Calculate the point-biserial correlation

As noted above, the point-biserial correlation is a special case of Pearson correlation. But how can we calculate Pearson correlation when one variable is nominal? Let's look at an example.

Let's say we want to study the correlation between the number of hours spent studying for an exam and the exam result (pass/fail).

keenable.title: Exact rational certificates and a Lean formalization of the eleven-variable Vasc inequality
keenable.snippet: We prove that the cyclic sum $\sum_{i=0}^{10}(x_i-x_{i+1})/(x_{i+1}+x_{i+2})$ is nonnegative for every strictly positive real eleven-tuple, with indices taken modulo eleven. Clearing denominators reduces the problem to a homogeneous polynomial. Subtracting the smallest coordinate then separates the proof into nonnegativity of a common-translation derivative and nonnegativity on a full boundary face. We supply exact rational polynomial certificates in Gram-matrix form for both statements. The derivative certificate uses a linear multiplier, centered monomials and cyclic averaging; the boundary certificate uses a strictly positive quadratic multiplier and uncentered monomials. Their verification requires 6,069 cyclic coefficient comparisons and 34,304 literal coefficient comparisons. All 606 certificate matrices are certified by integer congruences with strictly diagonally dominant images. A Lean 4 development formally verifies the certificate checks and their connection to the original inequality. The exact certificate data, replay programs, and formal sources are publicly available.

keenable.title: Structure and Exact Certification of Nonnegative Tensor Decompositions
keenable.snippet: We study the structure and exact certification of nonnegative tensor decompositions supplied through rational factor matrices. Every failure of minimality or essential uniqueness contains an irreducible positive exchange between p supplied terms and q competing terms. The exponent is independent of the tensor order and the mode dimensions. For Lebesgue moment tensors, positive quadrature determines the nonnegative rank and the uniqueness behavior, and some rational length-R inputs force a common field of degree at least ⌊R/2⌋! for any exact minimum-length output. Title: A Proof of the Dittert Conjecture in Dimension 4 via an Exact Constrained Sum-of-Squares Certificate

Authors: Jinhui Li, Beibei Xiong, Zhengfeng Yang

View PDF HTML (experimental)

Abstract: The Dittert conjecture states that the Dittert functional on nonnegative $n\times n$ matrices whose entries sum to $n$ is uniquely maximized by the uniform matrix. We prove the conjecture in dimension $4$ . More precisely, let $K_4$ be the simplex of nonnegative $4\times4$ real matrices whose entries sum to $4$ , let $U_4$ be the uniform matrix, and let $\phi$ denote the Dittert functional. We establish $\frac{61}{32}-\phi(A)\ge \frac{1}{52}\|A-U_4\|_F^2$ for every $A\in K_4$ . Consequently, $U_4$ is the unique maximizer of $\phi$ on $K_4$ .
 The proof reduces the problem to an exact certification of the nonnegativity of a structured quartic polynomial in sixteen variables on a simplex. We develop a symbolic-numeric procedure for constructing an exact rational constrained sum-of-squares certificate. The procedure combines adaptive template selection with sequential rational recovery to handle singular Gram matrices and coupled SOS blocks arising from the constraint structure. The final certificate consists of a main SOS with $152$ positively weighted rational squares and $136$ smaller SOS blocks, each containing $16$ such squares. Exact $LDL^T$ decompositions and coefficient comparison over $\mathbb{Q}$ certify the polynomial identity. The resulting exact certificate is formally verified using the Lean proof assistant.

Ptolemy’s inequality is a classic relationship between the distances among four points in Euclidean space. Another relationship between six distances is the 4-point condition, an inequality satisfied by the lengths of the six paths that join any four points of a metric (or weighted) tree. ## Correlation Matrices and Their Mathematical Properties

If you are a quant finance learner, you have almost certainly filled in a correlation matrix by hand: a stress scenario, a Monte Carlo input, a homework covariance model. Every number looked sensible. Then a Cholesky routine crashed, or a risk report printed a negative variance, and nothing obvious was wrong. The problem is that a correlation matrix is not a table of independent numbers. Its entries constrain each other, and a matrix can have every entry between $-1$ and $1$ and still describe a world that cannot exist.

This post is a checklist. It lists every property a valid correlation matrix must satisfy, says exactly how to check each one, and shows what "passes" looks like. seltz.snippet:
**The phi coefficient (φ) is the correlation measure for two binary (dichotomous) variables** — it is what you get when you compute a Pearson correlation on two variables that each take only two values (yes/no, present/absent, exposed/unexposed). It is not a separate statistic invented for categorical data: it is derived directly from the same 2×2 chi-square test of independence you would run on the same table, and it is numerically identical to Pearson’s *r* computed on the raw 0/1-coded data. This page covers the exact formula, that identity with chi-square and Pearson’s *r*, and a property that surprises people who treat φ as a plain correlation coefficient: when the two variables have unequal marginal distributions — one category much rarer than the other — φ cannot reach 1 even for the strongest association the data could possibly show.

## What phi measures

Phi applies specifically to a 2×2 contingency table: two variables, each with exactly two categories. Label the cells *a*, *b*, *c*, *d* as below:

|   | Variable 2 = present | Variable 2 = absent | Row total |
| -- | -------------------- | ------------------- | --------- |
| Variable 1 = present | a | b | a + b |
| Variable 1 = absent | c | d | c + d |
| Column total | a + c | b + d | n |

Phi can be computed two equivalent ways. Directly from the cell counts:

**φ = (ad − bc) / √[(a+b)(c+d)(a+c)(b+d)]**

Or from the table’s own chi-square statistic and sample size:

**φ = √(χ² / n)**

These two formulas always agree — the second is just the first with the numerator and denominator both expressed through χ². Because a square root is always non-negative, the chi-square-based formula on its own only gives you the magnitude of φ; the sign (direction of the association) comes from whether *ad* is greater or less than *bc* in the direct formula.

seltz.snippet:
A correlation table arrives in an analytical handover looking reassuringly ordinary. It is square, symmetric, finite, and accompanied by counts that appear consistent. Before it becomes an input to another analysis, however, a reviewer asks a more operational question: **which source records produced each coefficient?**

That question matters because pandas.DataFrame.corr() does not require every coefficient to use one shared set of rows. In pandas 2.2.3, Pearson correlation is computed from pairwise complete observations: each column pair can therefore use its own observed-row intersection. min_periods supplies a minimum observation count for each pair, but it does not establish that different pairs used the same record identities.

This article audits that boundary with owned synthetic float64 DataFrames containing three selected features, x, y, and z, plus stable string record IDs. The central decision is not whether pairwise correlation is intrinsically acceptable or whether complete-case selection is intrinsically superior. It is whether the evidence satisfies the **declared sample contract**.

The workflow therefore records pair memberships, preserves excluded records, builds a separately declared common-cohort candidate when required, and distinguishes computational eligibility from analytical approval. The controls deliberately include a finite pairwise matrix with different source IDs, a complete four-row identity-matrix control, and a twelve-row pair-only identity-matrix counterexample. Matrix appearance is evidence about the numbers; row identity is evidence about the sample.

Before reading any coefficient, write down five things: the selected features (x, y, z), the record-identity field, the Pearson method, the missing-observation rule, and the intended sample policy. That declaration turns “run corr()” into a reviewable analytical contract.

seltz.snippet: Suppose you measure the height and weight of many adults. Or the temperature and ice-cream sales on many days. You suspect these pairs of numbers move together. But "moving together" is a vague idea until it is made precise. Covariance and correlation are the two standard tools that quantify this tendency. They measure how two random variables increase or decrease together. This turns an intuitive notion of association into a computable, provably well-behaved number. The idea matters because almost every question in applied probability and statistics involving more than one random variable reduces at some point to computing or bounding a covariance. This includes portfolio risk, regression, principal component analysis, and the variance of a sum of dependent random variables. Covariance is the natural "cross term" that appears whenever we expand Var(X+Y)\mathrm{Var}(X+Y). Correlation is its normalized, unit-free version. It is bounded between −1-1 and 11, which allows comparison across different scales of measurement. The big picture is that covariance is a bilinear form on random variables. It is much like an inner product on a vector space. This algebraic structure is exactly what makes it tractable. It obeys clean symmetry and linearity rules. These rules let us compute variances of complicated linear combinations from simple pairwise pieces. Correlation is the corresponding "cosine of the angle" between two random variables in this inner-product geometry. The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality underlies its boundedness. ultimate.snippet: We prove that the cyclic sum $\sum_{i=0}^{10}(x_i-x_{i+1})/(x_{i+1}+x_{i+2})$ is nonnegative for every strictly positive real eleven-tuple, with indices taken modulo eleven. Clearing denominators reduces the problem to a homogeneous polynomial. Subtracting the smallest coordinate then separates the proof into nonnegativity of a common-translation derivative and nonnegativity on a full boundary face. We supply exact rational polynomial certificates in Gram-matrix form for both statements. The derivative certificate uses a linear multiplier, centered monomials and cyclic averaging; the boundary certificate uses a strictly positive quadratic multiplier and uncentered monomials. Their verification requires 6,069 cyclic coefficient comparisons and 34,304 literal coefficient comparisons. All 606 certificate matrices are certified by integer congruences with strictly diagonally dominant images. A Lean 4 development formally verifies the certificate checks and their connection to the original inequality. The exact certificate data, replay programs, and formal sources are publicly available.

webiq.snippet: Ptolemy’s inequality is a classic relationship between the distances among four points in Euclidean space. Another relationship between six distances is the 4-point condition, an inequality satisfied by the lengths of the six paths that join any four points of a metric (or weighted) tree.
